store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to have come so far from my intro classes on simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basic quantum computing. It's amazing how quickly time has passed.
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a fan of theory when it directly applies to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The concepts can be mind-bending, but it's a good kind of challenging. Our professor is great at explaining these complex ideas in an intuitive way. She'll present a problem that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my mind is buzzing.
store.2: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second most challenging. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with team members who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about the final product. However, that's also the beauty of it. In real-world settings, you're never working in isolation. You need to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures with ease. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed it and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. My professor is from the industry and worked on a couple of indie games that did well. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even some user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. In the last one, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced. However, the professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than just math. We do use linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're exploring algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing and has changed the way I approach problems.
store.5: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is essentially the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and staying organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all the agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective, Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding in my other classes. It's nice to sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: I'm juggling a typical college schedule. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it adds to the workload.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, more if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time-sink. My group meets at least twice a week, and we rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare. Despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a job environment.
store.9: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially if something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's no longer as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, collaborate, and think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.
store.10: So, that's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I can't imagine my undergrad years without it—it's definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
